No pressure.

Just information I wish every patient had before they let someone cut them open.

Sometimes healing doesn't come from the scalpel.

Sometimes, it comes from giving your shoulder the blood flow to breathe again.

title: Tingling in your hands… what’s really going on?
body:
I sat in my pickup truck and watched my best friend's funeral procession ride past me.
42 motorcycles.
I should have been the second one back.
I drove the F-150 instead.
And what happened three weeks after that funeral is the only reason I'm writing this.
Because if Ray hadn't died - if Frank hadn't been at that wake - I'd still be sitting on my back porch listening to other men ride past my house on Sunday mornings.
I want to say something to every man my age who's quietly given up on something he loved.
Because I almost did.
—
I bought my first Harley in 1991.
A Sportster. Used. Broke down on me twice the first month.
I didn't care.
I rode it to work every day from April to October for fourteen years.
I rode to the Black Hills every August. 24 years in a row.
Ray and me and four other guys - we'd leave from the diner at 5am on the second Saturday and we'd be in Sturgis by Tuesday afternoon.
24 years.
That's not a hobby.
That's who I was.
—
I ran a small machine shop. Retired four years ago.
The day after I retired, I bought a 2018 Road King. Black on black.
The bike I'd been promising myself for 30 years.
I rode it home from the dealership and pulled into the driveway and my wife came out and said "well there he is."
She meant it nicely.
I knew what she meant.
The plan was simple. Retire. Ride. Take the grandkids out on Saturdays when they got old enough. Do the Black Hills run with Ray every summer until one of us couldn't.
That was the plan.
—
The first time I noticed something was wrong, I was tightening a fitting on a hose in my garage.
Saturday morning. October. I'd just come back from a 90-minute ride.
I picked up a 1/2 inch wrench and my right hand wouldn't close around it.
Like a switch had flipped.
I just stood there in the garage looking at my own hand like it belonged to somebody else.
I shook it out. Ran some hot water over it. It loosened up after about 20 minutes.
I told myself it was just a long ride. Cold morning. I was 58.
These things happen.
—
But it kept happening.
It happened the next Saturday.
Then the Saturday after that.
Then it started happening on weekday mornings before I'd even ridden anywhere.
I'd wake up at 6am and lie in bed flexing my right hand under the covers trying to make the joints work.
The base of my thumb felt like it was full of broken glass.
I started pre-heating my coffee mug in the microwave.
Not the coffee - the mug.
So when I picked it up the warmth would loosen the joint enough to grip it.
I never told anyone I was doing that.
It felt like an old man thing to do.
I was 59.
—
By the next spring it was bad.
I'd grip the handlebars at 7am for the morning ride and 20 minutes in my right hand would start cramping around the throttle.
I'd shift my position. Stretch the fingers out at red lights. Try to ride one-handed for stretches to give it a break.
The boys started noticing.
Ray pulled up next to me at a gas station outside Mansfield and said: "you alright over there?"
I said yeah. Just a cramp.
He looked at me for a long second.
He didn't say anything else.
But I knew he knew.
—
I went to my GP.
He looked at my hand and said the words I'd been dreading.
"Looks like CMC joint arthritis. Base of the thumb. Pretty common in guys who use their hands for a living."
He prescribed Meloxicam.
I took it for six months.
It helped a little. It also gave me an ulcer.
I had to stop.
—
Then I started the parade.
Don't laugh.
You probably did the same parade.
I tried over-the-counter ibuprofen. Three a day. Stomach turned to acid in two weeks.
I tried a wrist brace from CVS. Felt better wearing it but I couldn't ride with it on - couldn't get good throttle control. And when I took it off, the wrist had gotten weaker. So that was a wash.
I tried a cortisone shot. The orthopedic guy stuck a needle right into the joint. Hurt like hell.
But for about three weeks I felt 25 years old.
Then it wore off.
He said I could get one more, maybe two, but cortisone breaks down the cartilage long term. He said: "you don't want to be doing these every six weeks."
I tried glucosamine and chondroitin. The big bottle from Costco. Took it religiously for four months.
Maybe a tiny difference. Hard to say.
I tried turmeric capsules because my niece swore by them.
Nothing I could feel.
I tried CBD oil - both the topical and the gummies. Spent like $180 on a bottle of the topical because my buddy said it was "the real stuff."
Nothing.
I tried hot wax dips. Compression gloves. A TENS machine I bought off Amazon for $89.
Nothing. Nothing. Nothing.
—
I'd seen the copper bracelet ads.
I'd scrolled past them a hundred times.
Every time I saw one I'd say the same thing out loud: "what a load of garbage."
Copper bracelets are something women in the 1970s wore.
Something my grandma had in a drawer.
Snake oil for old people who'd given up.
Not me.
I was a machinist. I'd worked with metals for 35 years. I knew copper.
Copper is for wire and pipe and decorative pots.
Copper is not medicine.
I would never have bought one.
Not in a million years.
—
By the time I was 61 I was not riding anymore.
Not really.
I'd take the bike out of the garage on Sundays and ride for 20 minutes around the block to keep the battery up.
Then I'd put it back.
I missed the Black Hills run that summer.
First time in 25 years.
I told the guys it was because my wife had a thing.
She didn't have a thing.
I just couldn't grip the bars for the 18 hours of riding it would take to get there.
I cried in the garage that Saturday morning while everyone else left at 5am.
I don't tell people that.
I haven't told my wife.
I'm telling you because I think there's somebody reading this who's done the same thing.
Sat in your garage on the morning your boys left without you.
—
I listed the Road King on Marketplace twice.
Both times I took it down before anybody messaged me.
I couldn't bring myself to sell it.
But I couldn't ride it either.
So it sat there.
Eight thousand miles on a 2018.
You don't see that on a bike that belongs to a man who's been riding for 30 years.
That bike was a tombstone in my garage.
—
And then in November Ray died.
Heart attack.
He was 64.
He was on his bike when it happened. Pulled over to the shoulder of Route 30. Made the call to 911 himself.
Was gone before the EMTs got there.
The boys planned the procession for the funeral.
42 bikes. From the funeral home to the cemetery. 90 minutes through three towns.
I was supposed to be second back, behind Ray's son.
The night before the funeral I sat in my garage and tried to grip the handlebars of the Road King for 30 seconds.
I couldn't.
After 15 seconds my right hand was a claw.
I drove the F-150 to the funeral.
I parked it on the side of the road outside the cemetery and I sat there and I watched 41 bikes ride past me.
41 because mine was the missing one.
I cried in that truck.
For Ray.
For me.
For the man I used to be who was dead too - just nobody had buried him yet.
—
After the service there's a wake at the VFW.
I'm standing in the corner with a cup of coffee I can't grip properly.
A guy walks up to me.
Big guy. Beard. Late 50s. Riding gear under his suit jacket.
He sticks out his hand.
"Frank Kowalski. I rode with Ray's brother in the 90s."
I shake his hand.
I notice he has a copper bracelet on his right wrist.
I notice it the way you notice things you've been dismissing your whole life.
He sees me notice.
He says: "you're Mike, right? Ray told me about you. Said you were having hand trouble."
I say yeah.
He says: "what kind?"
I tell him. CMC joint. Base of the thumb. Bone on bone now.
He nods.
He says: "I'm a hand surgeon. I work out of the orthopedic group on East Main. You should come see me Monday."
He hands me a card.
I'm thinking great. Another guy who's going to tell me about cortisone or fusion surgery.
I almost throw the card away in the parking lot.
I don't know why I didn't.
—
Monday morning I'm sitting in Frank's exam room.
He's not in scrubs. He's in jeans and a flannel.
He looks at my hand for about two minutes. Pushes on the joint. Has me grip his finger. Watches me try to twist a doorknob he keeps in his desk drawer for testing range of motion.
He sits down across from me.
He says: "alright. Let me tell you what I'd tell my own brother."
He held up one finger.
"You have stage 3 CMC arthritis. Bone on bone. 30 years of gripping handlebars and machine tools. The cartilage is gone. It's not coming back."
I felt my stomach drop.
Then he held up a second finger.

"Surgery is an option. I'd do it if I thought it was your best option. But I'm going to tell you something most surgeons won't. 

For guys like you - riders, guys who use their hands hard - surgery on the CMC joint trades a known pain for an unknown outcome. 

About 60% of riders I've operated on say they wish they'd waited. The grip strength after surgery is permanently reduced.

You wouldn't be back on a Road King doing 18 hour days. Not the same way. So if you're asking me, I'm telling you I'd do it last. Not first."

I said okay.

Then he held up a third finger.

He said: "the next thing I'm going to tell you most doctors won't say. Most doctors won't say it because they can't bill for it and they can't prove it in a study yet. 

But I've been a hand surgeon for 23 years. And I've watched too many of my patients walk out of here, dismiss my advice, and come back six months later with less pain than I could have given them. So I track what works."

He pulled up his sleeve.

The copper bracelet on his right wrist.

"This is mine," he said. "I've been wearing it for four years. And I tell every single one of my CMC patients about it. Not because I sell it. I don't. Not because I have a study to wave at you. I don't. But because the data I have - my own patients, hundreds of them - is too consistent to ignore."
—

I just stared at him.

He said: "let me tell you what I think is happening. I don't fully know. But here's what I know."
He drew a circle on his notepad.

"Your CMC joint is inflamed. Chronic, low-grade inflammation. The cartilage is gone. Every time you grip something - handlebars, a wrench, a coffee mug - bone rubs on bone, the inflammation goes up, the joint stiffens, you lose more range of motion, and you grip harder to compensate. Which makes the inflammation worse."

He tapped the circle.

"Cycle. It feeds itself. That's what you've been living in for four years."
He continued.

"Your pills. Meloxicam. Ibuprofen. Those work by blocking the chemical signal of inflammation. They don't reduce the inflammation itself. They mute the alarm. They don't put out the fire. And they trash your gut and your kidneys doing it."

I thought about my ulcer.

"The wrist brace. It immobilizes the joint, which gives the inflammation a chance to drop. But it also makes the muscles around it weaker, so when you take it off, you're worse than before. And you can't ride with it on."
I nodded.

"The cortisone. Cortisone is a hammer. It crushes inflammation for three weeks. Then it wears off and the joint comes back angrier - and the cortisone itself accelerates cartilage breakdown. I do them. I do them sparingly. They are not a long-term solution."

He paused.

"The supplements - glucosamine, turmeric, CBD. There's some signal in the literature. Tiny effect. Months to feel it if at all. None of them are doing anything significant for stage 3 CMC."

He looked at me.

"Everything you've tried addresses one piece of this cycle. Or zero. None of them break it. So the inflammation keeps cycling. The grip keeps weakening. The joint keeps degrading. And four years go by."

I sat there.
I had nothing to say.
Because I'd just heard the first explanation in five years that actually made sense.
—
I asked the question.
"So what does the bracelet do?"
He smiled. Like he was waiting for it.
He said: "I'll give you the honest answer. Three things are probably happening. Maybe one. Maybe all three. The science isn't settled, and I'm not going to lie to you and pretend it is."
He held up one finger.

"Trace copper absorption through the skin. Copper is an essential mineral. It's a cofactor in the enzymes that build collagen and reduce inflammation. People with arthritis tend to be low in copper. Wearing pure solid copper against the skin appears to deliver trace amounts trans-dermally. Modest. Real."

Two fingers.

"Magnetic field interaction with local circulation. The neodymium magnets in a real medical-grade copper bracelet - not the cheap plated stuff - appear to dilate micro-vessels around the joint. More circulation, less inflammation, more debris cleared. There are studies on this. They're not slam-dunk. But they're not nothing."
Three fingers.

"And honestly - there's probably a placebo effect on top of both of those. And I want you to know I do not care. Because here's the thing every doctor learns and most won't say out loud. Placebo isn't fake. Placebo is your nervous system deciding to dial down a pain signal. That's a real biological event. If a $30 piece of copper convinces your nervous system to release the chronic guarding response in your hand, the cartilage doesn't care why. It just gets a break."

I laughed. First time in two months.
He said: "I'm a surgeon. I trust what I can cut into. But I also trust 4,000 hand patients telling me the same thing for 23 years. So when I have a guy like you - stage 3, riding, surgery is the wrong first step - I tell you to try this for three months before we talk about anything else."
—
I said: "but every copper bracelet I've ever seen looks like junk."
He said: "they are junk. 95% of them."
He opened his desk drawer.
He pulled out a small box.
He said: "the only one I've found that's worth a damn is this brand. Pure solid copper - most of the ones online are copper-plated zinc and they turn your wrist green in a week and they don't do anything because zinc isn't copper. This one is solid copper through and through. With actual neodymium magnets, not the weak stuff. Premium build that holds up to manual work. Comes with a sizing tool - you can adjust it yourself."
He set it on the desk.
The brand was called Willis Judd.
I'd never heard of it.
He said: "wear it 24/7 for three weeks. Don't take it off. Then I want you to take it off for one full day in week four and tell me what happens."
I asked why.
He said: "because that's how you'll know if it's doing something. The removal test. If the pain comes back when you take it off and goes away when you put it back on, you have your answer. If nothing changes, send it back. They have a 60 day money back guarantee. You're out the time it takes to mail it."
I ordered it from his office on my phone.
—
Week one.
Honestly?
Not much.
I kept waiting to feel something. I don't know what I was expecting. A tingle. A hum.
Nothing.
Maybe my hand felt slightly looser in the morning. Maybe I was imagining it.
I almost took it off twice.
But Frank's voice was in my head. Three weeks. Don't judge it.
So I kept it on.
—
Week two.
Tuesday morning. 6am.
I came down to the kitchen to make coffee.
I picked up the mug.
Cold mug. No microwave.
And I gripped it.
Just like that.
I stood in the kitchen holding a cold coffee mug and I started crying.
Because I'd forgotten that pre-heating the mug wasn't a normal thing.
I'd forgotten what it felt like to grip something cold first thing in the morning without flinching.
It came back to me in that one second.
My wife came in. Saw my face.
She said "what's wrong?"
I held up the mug.
I said: "nothing. Nothing's wrong."
—
-Week three.
I went into the garage.
I pulled the cover off the Road King.
I sat on it. Both hands on the bars.
I gripped the throttle.
I held it.
20 seconds.
30 seconds.
A minute.
It didn't claw up.
I sat there in the garage with my hands on the bars of a bike I hadn't really ridden in 18 months and I realized I was shaking.
I started it up.
Took it down the driveway.
Around the block.
Came back.
Hands felt fine.
—
Week four.
I did the test.
Saturday morning. Took the bracelet off. Left it on my dresser.
Drove to the lake with my wife. Spent the day fishing.
By 2pm my right hand was cramping again.
By 4pm I couldn't grip the steering wheel without shifting my grip every five minutes.
We drove home.
I put the bracelet back on at 6pm.
By 9pm I was fine.
That was the moment I knew.
It wasn't placebo. Or - fine. Maybe it was. I don't care.
It worked.
That's all I care about.
—
Week six.
I rode the Saturday morning loop with the boys.
Two hours.
Three of the four guys are still alive.
We rode past the cemetery where Ray is buried.
I waved.
Felt stupid. Did it anyway.
When we pulled into the diner I got off the bike and I shook out my hand and it was fine.
Tom looked at me from the next bike.
He said: "you're back."
I just nodded.
I couldn't say anything.
—
Week eight.
Two months ago last Tuesday.
I rode to the Black Hills.
I made the boys leave a day later than usual so I could go.
Five days. Eighteen-hour ride days.
My grandson rode behind me on the back seat for the first time. He's 14.
His mom - my daughter - texted me a picture of us pulling out of the driveway at 5am.
Two helmets. The Road King. The sun coming up.
She wrote: "dad you look like you again."
I cried in a gas station in Iowa reading that text.
I'm a 62 year old man crying in a Casey's at 9am.
I don't care.
—
I'm writing this six months after Ray's funeral.
I'm wearing the bracelet right now.
I haven't taken it off in 178 days except for that one day at the lake and a couple of times to shower.
My hand is not perfect.
The cartilage is still gone. I still have stiffness if I really push it.
But I'm riding.
I'm gripping wrenches in the garage again.
I opened a pickle jar on Sunday.
My wife was in the kitchen. She just looked at me when I handed it back to her open.
She said "well look at you."
I winked at her.
I haven't winked at my wife in four years.
—
I'm writing this because I almost gave up.
I almost sold the Road King.
I almost spent the rest of my riding years sitting on the porch listening to other men ride past.
And the only reason I didn't is because Ray died and Frank was at the wake and I happened to take the card.
I want there to be one less Mike in a pickup truck at his buddy's funeral procession.
If you're reading this and your hand is the reason you're not riding anymore - or your shoulder is the reason you don't golf anymore - or your wrist is the reason you don't garden anymore -
I'm not telling you copper is magic.
I'm telling you this is what worked for me.
And the worst case is you're out the time to mail it back.
—
It's called Willis Judd.
Pure solid copper. Real neodymium magnets. Comes with a sizing tool so the clasp doesn't fight you.
60 day money-back guarantee. I checked. They actually honor it. Frank's patients have tested.
Wear it 24/7 for three weeks before you decide.
Then take it off for a day in week four and see what your body tells you.
That's the test.
—
I'm not a doctor.
I'm not a salesman.
I'm a 62 year old retired machinist who almost gave up and didn't.
Ray didn't get any more rides.
I did.
Don't sit in your truck while your buddies ride past.
Don't list the bike on Marketplace twice and take it down twice.
Don't tell yourself this is just what 60 looks like.
Try the thing.
Wear it for three weeks.
Take it off for a day.
Let your body tell you what your nervous system already knows.
I rode 1,400 miles last month.
A year ago I couldn't grip a coffee mug.
That's all I have to say.

title: Why Your Hips Ache Every Night
body:
Twelve doctor appointments.

Two MRIs, one CT scan, countless X-rays.

And not a single doctor thought to ask me one simple question.

The question that would have explained everything.

The question that took me YEARS to figure out. 

========

I'm 54. And for the past three years, I've been fighting a hip pain that no one could properly diagnose. 

And honestly? I was starting to think I was losing my mind.

It started small. Just this stabbing ache on the outside of my hip after my morning walks. The kind of thing you brush off. Slept wrong. Need new shoes. Finally feeling my age.

But it didn't go away. It got worse.

The pain started waking me up at night. I'd lie on my left side and within minutes, this deep burning pressure would build.

Like someone slowly pressing their thumb into the bone, harder and harder until I couldn't take it anymore. I'd flip to my right side. Twenty minutes later, same thing. Flip again. Left side. Right side. Stare at the ceiling. Try my back. 

My husband started calling me a rotisserie chicken.

I laughed the first few times. By month four, I wanted to throw my pillow at his head.

========

Here's what no one tells you about chronic pain: 

It's not just the pain. It's everything the pain takes from you.

By month six, I was averaging maybe three hours of broken sleep. I'd drag myself out of bed feeling like I'd aged twenty years overnight — this deep stiffness that took a full ten minutes of shuffling around the bedroom before I could walk normally. 

Stairs became something I had to psych myself up for. That shooting ache down my outer thigh with every single step. I started planning my whole day around avoiding them.

I stopped going to my Thursday morning yoga class. Cancelled on my sister's birthday dinner. Skipped my nephew's soccer games because the metal bleachers were agony and standing on the sidelines wasn't much better.

I was becoming the woman who always had a reason she couldn't come.

That wasn't who I was. I used to be the one organizing things. Dragging everyone out for hikes. First one on the dance floor at weddings, last one to leave. I once walked nine miles through Rome in a single day just because I didn't want to miss anything.

Now I was the one people had learned to stop inviting.

========

And the nights... God, the nights were the worst.

I'd lie there in the dark, brain spinning out of control, convinced something was seriously wrong. Bone cancer. A tumor. Some degenerative disease quietly eating away at my hip socket while doctors kept telling me everything looked "normal." I'd catastrophize for hours while the pain pulsed and my husband slept peacefully six inches away.

One night — maybe month eight or nine, I'd stopped keeping track by then — he rolled over and put his arm around me. This thing he's done for twenty-three years of marriage. His hand rested on my hip, gentle, half-asleep.

And I flinched. Pulled away. Couldn't help it. Even that soft pressure was too much.

He didn't say anything. But I saw his face in the glow of the alarm clock.

I still think about that look.

We don't really touch anymore. Not like we used to. And I can't tell if it's because I've pulled away so many times he's stopped trying, or because I've started preemptively angling my body away from him in bed, protecting that hip like it's made of glass.

Probably both.

========

That was the week I finally went to my doctor.

She pressed on my hip, asked if it hurt here (yes), here (god yes), and here (I nearly levitated off the table). She nodded like she'd solved a puzzle.

"Bursitis. Pretty common at your age. Take ibuprofen, ice it, should calm down in a few weeks."

It didn't.

Two months later, I was back. She referred me to an orthopedist.

He squinted at my X-rays for maybe sixty seconds while I sat there in that paper gown, feeling like a specimen.

"Some arthritis. Normal wear and tear. You're what, mid-fifties?" He said it like that explained everything. "We can try cortisone if the ibuprofen isn't cutting it."

The first injection actually helped. For about three weeks, I felt almost normal. Slept on my side two nights in a row. Started making plans again.

Then it came back. Worse somehow.

Second injection lasted maybe ten days. Third one might as well have been saline.

I went to another orthopedist — paid $400 out of pocket because supposedly he was "the best." Same answer. Arthritis. Wear and tear. "Have you considered physical therapy?"

So I tried it. Twice a week for two months. Clamshells, bridges, resistance bands, stretches that were supposed to "strengthen the stabilizers."

But every night, the pain was the same. Sometimes worse — there were days after PT when I could barely make it up my front steps.

When I told my therapist it wasn't helping, she looked almost hurt. "You have to trust the process."

I stopped going after ten weeks. Couldn't justify the copays for something that wasn't working.

Here's the thing about pain that doesn't show up on tests: doctors start looking at you differently.

You can see it. The slight skepticism. The barely-hidden impatience. The unspoken suggestion that maybe you're exaggerating. 

One doctor asked if I'd "considered talking to someone." Took me a second to realize he meant a therapist.

I drove home and sat in my car in the driveway for twenty minutes, engine off, just staring at my garage door. Wondering if this was just my life now. Wondering if I really was being dramatic. Wondering if everyone was right and I just needed to accept that this is what fifty-four feels like.

Wondering how many more years of this I could actually survive.

That was my lowest point.

========

Here's what I need you to understand about those three years and twelve appointments:

Every single doctor asked me the same questions.

Where does it hurt? How long has it been going on? Does it radiate? Any numbness or tingling? What makes it worse? What makes it better? Any injuries? What's your activity level? Family history of arthritis?

They asked about my weight. My exercise habits. My stress levels. Whether I'd tried yoga. Whether I'd tried losing weight. Whether I'd tried "just resting it."

But not ONE of them — not my GP, not the orthopedists, not the physical therapist, not the rheumatologist — asked me the question that actually mattered:

When did this start relative to my menopause?

It never even occurred to me to connect the two. Why would it?

Everyone warns you about the hot flashes. The night sweats. The mood swings. The brain fog. The weight that suddenly clings to your midsection no matter what you eat.

But hip pain that feels like someone's driving a railroad spike into your outer thigh every time you try to sleep on your side?

Nobody mentions that. It's not in any of the menopause pamphlets. Your gynecologist doesn't bring it up. Your friends complain about hot flashes over wine — nobody's talking about their hips.

So I never made the connection.

Until 2:47 AM on a Tuesday.

I remember the exact time because I'd been watching the clock for hours. 

I was scrolling through my phone because sleep wasn't coming and I needed something to do besides lie there counting the ways my body had failed me.

And I found this video from a menopause researcher.

I almost kept scrolling. I'd watched dozens of videos by then. Read hundreds of articles. Tried every stretch, every supplement, every sleeping position anyone had ever suggested. None of them told me anything useful.

But something made me click. Maybe it was the 2 AM desperation. Maybe I was just too tired to keep scrolling. Maybe some part of me wasn't ready to give up yet.

Whatever it was, I'm grateful for it every single day.

Because about two minutes in, this researcher asked a question that made my whole body go still.

"Did your pain start around or after menopause?"

I paused the video.

Sat up in bed. Hip screaming at the sudden movement, but I barely noticed.

Did it?

I tried to remember. When did this really start? Not the bad pain — the early stuff. The first time I noticed something wasn't quite right.

I thought back. When did I first start waking up stiff? When did stairs first become a thing I noticed? When did I first feel that weird ache after a long walk?

And I realized: it was about eight months after my periods stopped completely. Right around the time I'd finally accepted that menopause was "over" and I could stop thinking about it.

I'd never connected those two things.

In three years of doctors and tests and failed treatments, I'd never once thought: wait. This started right after menopause. Is that a coincidence?

And nobody — not a single medical professional — had ever suggested it might not be.

I pressed play.

And what this researcher explained over the next ten minutes:

About what's actually happening inside the hip during and after menopause.

========

I'm not going to tell you this video will be your answer. I don't know your body. I don't know your situation. I don't know what's causing your specific pain.

But I know this:

If you've been fighting hip pain that doesn't show up on X-rays...

If doctors keep calling it arthritis or bursitis while the treatments don't work...

If you've started wondering whether you're just being dramatic, whether this is just "getting older," whether you should just accept it and stop complaining...

Watch this video.

It's about ten minutes. It might be the first thing about your hip pain that actually makes sense.

I'm not saying that to sell you anything. I'm saying it because I spent three years in pain when I didn't have to. Three years of my life. Three years of sleep. Three years of slowly pulling away from my husband, my friends, myself.

I don't want that for you.

Click below. Watch it tonight.

And maybe, FINALLY, you'll have the answer to the question no one thought to ask.

title: The Real Reason Your Migraines Keep Coming Back (It’s Not What You Think)
body:
I tracked my migraines for 2,190 days.
It took me six years to realize I was treating the pain, not the source.
Every morning, same ritual. Eyes still closed. Is it there? The pressure behind my right eye. The tightness wrapping around my temple. The dull throb at the base of my skull that tells me today is already ruined.
Day 2,190. Level 7. Again.
My daughter stopped asking if I'm coming to her games. She just assumes I'm not. I stopped promising years ago because breaking a promise to your child is worse than just being absent.
The doctors called me a "chronic, treatment-resistant migraine patient." Like I'm the problem. Like my body is doing this on purpose.
I lay there one morning staring at six years of data in my migraine app. Every single day logged. Pain levels, triggers, medications, sleep quality, barometric pressure, hormone cycles, food diaries. Everything documented. And I still wake up exactly the same.
The first neurologist put me on Topamax. It made me forget words mid-sentence. My coworkers thought I was having a stroke. Still had the migraines. Then Propranolol. Blood pressure dropped so low I fainted in a grocery store. Then Amitriptyline. Gained 30 pounds and slept 14 hours a day. Then combinations of all three at once.
Triptans were supposed to be the rescue. They worked for the first few months. Then I needed them more often. Then I needed them every other day. Nobody told me that taking them more than three times a week could actually cause MORE migraines. I found out later it has a name: Medication Overuse Headache.
I was taking the thing that was supposed to save me, and it was making me worse.
Botox was next. Thirty-one injection sites across my forehead, temples, and neck every twelve weeks. I sat in that chair with needles in my face thinking: this is what my life has become. Five rounds later, nothing changed. But I kept going back because what else was I going to do?
The three-day inpatient stay at the headache center cost me my savings. IV infusions. Nerve blocks that made me sob in the recovery room. Medication combinations I can't pronounce. They tried everything in their protocol.
On day two, the attending came in and said they'd "exhausted their acute options." I went home and added it to my spreadsheet. Treatment #34: Failed.
My husband thinks I'm not trying hard enough. My friends stopped inviting me out around year two. How do you explain to someone that you've done everything, literally everything, and you're still in the same bed, curtains drawn, ice pack on your face, at 2pm on a Saturday?
I keep tracking because I don't know what else to do. Maybe if I log enough data, someone will finally see what I can't.
It wasn't until month 73 that someone finally explained what was actually happening.
Not the neurologist. Not the headache specialist. Not the ER doctor who'd seen me four times that year.
It was a migraine coach I almost didn't call because I thought it was a waste of money.
She listened to me for twenty minutes. Didn't interrupt once. Then she asked me one question:
"When do you take your medication?"
I told her I wait. Like everyone does. I wait until it's a 6 or 7, until I can't push through anymore, and then I take a Triptan or Excedrin.
She went quiet for a moment.
"That's the problem. Every single treatment you've tried: the pills, the injections, the infusions, they're all trying to stop a migraine that's already fully activated. But a migraine doesn't start with pain. Pain is the last stage."
I stared at my phone.
"Your migraine starts 20 to 40 minutes before you ever feel the headache. It starts with nerve sensitization. The trigeminal nerve, it runs from the base of your skull up through your temples and behind your eyes. When it gets activated, it sends pain signals cascading through your head. By the time you feel the throbbing, the nerve has been firing for almost an hour."
"Every medication you've taken has been trying to put out a fire that's been burning for 40 minutes before you even smell the smoke."
She told me about a topical formula developed by a neurologist who suffers from migraines herself. Dr. Flora Laurent. She'd spent years researching the trigeminal nerve pathway and found that specific compounds: Magnesium Glycinate, Wild Peppermint, Menthol Crystals, Chamomile, and Feverfew Extract, could be combined into a roll-on applied directly to the temples, neck, and behind the ears. Exactly where the trigeminal nerve surfaces closest to the skin.
It was called Florus Relief.
"It's not like anything you've tried," she said. "It doesn't enter your bloodstream. It doesn't pass through your liver. It works topically, right at the nerve pathway. The cooling sensation interrupts the pain signal at the surface while the magnesium and feverfew calm the nerve over time."
I almost laughed. A roll-on? After Botox? After nerve blocks? After thirty-four failed treatments?
But she explained it differently than anyone ever had.
"You don't have a medication problem. You have a timing and delivery problem. You've been swallowing pills that take 30 to 45 minutes to reach your bloodstream, by which point the migraine is fully established. And you've been doing it so often that your brain adapted to the medication and started producing rebound headaches. You need something that works in seconds, directly at the source, that you can use at the very first warning sign, without worrying about overuse."
I ordered it that night. Not because I believed it would work. I'd stopped believing anything would work around year three. But they had a 90-day guarantee and I was out of ideas.
It arrived two days later. Small green bottle. Metal roller ball. I held it in my hand and thought: how can something this simple fix what Botox couldn't?
The first migraine came three days later. I felt it starting the way it always does. The faint pressure behind my right eye. The slight neck stiffness. The beginning.
Instead of waiting. Instead of pushing through. Instead of reaching for the pill bottle.
I rolled it across my temples. Behind my ears. Down the back of my neck.
The cooling hit immediately. Not like an ice pack, gentler. Deeper. Like the tension was being drawn out of the nerve itself. Within minutes, the pressure eased. My shoulders dropped. The tightness behind my eye softened.
I sat there waiting for it to come back. Five minutes. Ten. Twenty.
It didn't fully disappear. But for the first time in six years, it didn't escalate.
The migraine that usually pins me to the bed for 8 hours peaked at a 3 and faded by lunch.
I opened my app. Day 2,194. Level 3. For the first time in years, I typed a number that didn't ruin my day.
That was five months ago.
I still track. But the numbers look different now. Most days are 0s and 1s. I catch it early, the second I feel the first whisper of pressure, I reach for the green bottle. Temples. Neck. Behind the ears. Ten seconds. And most of the time, that's it.
I took my daughter to her soccer game last Saturday. Sat in the sun for two hours. Cheered until my voice cracked. Didn't need the dark room after. Didn't cancel dinner.
She looked at me on the drive home and said, "Mom, you came to both games this week."
I had to pull over because I couldn't see through the tears.
I'm not "treatment-resistant." I never was. I was just delivering the wrong treatment, to the wrong place, at the wrong time.
If you've been tracking your migraines for months or years. If doctors have called you "chronic" or "resistant" or said "we've tried everything." If you wake up every morning doing the same check I do, scanning for the pain before you even open your eyes.
I need you to consider something.
What if you're not broken?
What if every pill failed because it was arriving 45 minutes too late to a nerve that needed relief in seconds? What if every injection failed because it was targeting the wrong layer? What if you've been treating a nerve problem with blood-level medications that never reach the nerve?
You can't swallow your way to relief from a nerve that fires at the surface of your skin. You can't wait until level 7 to treat something that started at level 1 forty minutes ago.
Florus Relief Roll-On was built for the moment the migraine begins, not the moment it's unbearable. Applied directly where the trigeminal nerve lives. Cooling relief in seconds, not 45 minutes.
7,405 migraine sufferers have rated it five stars. Developed by a Neurologist who gets migraines herself. And backed by a 90-day guarantee, feel relief or it's free.

title: This Changes Everything
body:
I found a lump on my granddaughter's neck, and it led me to discover what's really crawling on your family's produce.
 
The produce industry doesn't want you to know this.
 
And the companies selling you vinegar washes and twelve-dollar produce sprays are praying you never find out.
 
Hi, my name is Dakota, I'm a fifty-eight-year-old grandmother, and I've always prided myself on keeping a clean, welcoming kitchen.
 
The kind of home where my granddaughter Lily begged to stay for dinner and my husband Tom swore my cooking was the best in the county.
 
I bought fresh fruits and vegetables every week.
 
Rinsed everything under the tap before serving it.
 
I even kept a colander by the sink so I could rinse berries the second I got home from the store, just like my mother taught me.
 
But a few months ago, everything changed.
 
It started on a Saturday.
 
Lily had spent the afternoon at our house.
 
I made her favorite salad with spinach and strawberries and she snacked on grapes all afternoon.
 
She was fine.
 
Happy.
 
Normal.
 
Three days later, my daughter called.
 
Mom, Lily has a lump on her neck.
 
The doctor said it's a swollen lymph node.
 
My heart stopped.
 
He asked what she ate recently, my daughter continued.
 
I told him about the strawberries and grapes at your house.
 
There was a pause.
 
Then she said the words that kept me awake for three nights straight.
 
I'm not blaming you Mom, but the doctor said parasites and bacteria on produce can cause this in children.
 
My face went hot.
 
My hands were shaking.
 
I looked across the kitchen at the fruit bowl on the counter.
 
The same strawberries I had rinsed under the tap that morning.
 
The same grapes I thought were clean because I'd run water over them.
 
The same produce I thought was the healthiest thing I could feed my granddaughter.
 
Tom tried to calm me down.
 
Kids get swollen lymph nodes all the time, he said.
 
It could be anything.
 
But I couldn't let it go.
 
That night, after Tom went to bed, I started researching.
 
What I found kept me up until two in the morning.
 
And it wasn't just pesticides.
 
It was parasites.
 
Microscopic parasite eggs and larvae live on the surface of produce.
 
They come from contaminated soil. From irrigation water that contains animal waste. From workers handling food in fields with no sanitation. From shipping containers and conveyor belts that haven't been cleaned in months.
 
Roundworm. Hookworm. Tapeworm larvae. Toxoplasma. Cryptosporidium.
 
These aren't rare tropical diseases.
 
They are on grocery store produce in America right now.
 
The CDC estimates that more than sixty million Americans are carrying parasitic infections and most of them have no idea.
 
Because the symptoms don't look like parasites.
 
They look like bloating.
 
Stomach cramps.
 
Fatigue.
 
Swollen lymph nodes.
 
Unexplained weight changes.
 
Skin issues.
 
Brain fog.
 
Symptoms that doctors attribute to stress, diet, IBS, or age.
 
And the whole time, the actual cause is living in your gut, feeding off what you eat, because it hitched a ride on a strawberry you rinsed under the tap for three seconds.
 
A quick rinse under the tap removes maybe twenty to thirty percent of what's on your produce.
 
That's it.
 
Parasite eggs are microscopic.
 
They cling to the waxy surface of your produce.
 
They survive cold water.
 
They survive refrigeration.
 
Some of them survive stomach acid.
 
Running water over a strawberry was never going to wash off something designed by evolution to survive inside a human body.
 
And children are more vulnerable than adults.
 
Their immune systems are still developing.
 
Their smaller bodies can't fight off parasitic infections the way an adult can.
 
What gives a grown adult mild bloating can give a five-year-old swollen lymph nodes and a fever.
 
That's when the real panic set in.
 
The next morning, I watched Lily's little brother reach for a grape from the fruit bowl and I grabbed his hand before he could put it in his mouth.
 
I stared at the grape.
 
At the fruit bowl.
 
At the bag of spinach in the fridge.
 
In that moment, three things hit me at once.
 
This wasn't about dirty produce.
 
This wasn't coming off with water.
 
And this wasn't something I could keep ignoring.
 
That evening, I tried everything I could find.
 
First, the vinegar soak.
 
I mixed a solution in a bowl and dropped the strawberries in.
 
Twenty minutes later, the berries tasted like vinegar.
 
The kids wouldn't touch them.
 
And when I looked it up, vinegar doesn't kill parasite eggs.
 
It can weaken some bacteria on the outer surface but parasite eggs have a protective shell that vinegar cannot penetrate.
 
Next, baking soda.
 
Scrubbing each piece of produce by hand in a baking soda paste.
 
It took over twenty minutes to get through a single bowl of fruit.
 
Messy, tedious, and according to the research, it does not destroy parasitic organisms.
 
Tom tried a commercial produce wash spray he grabbed from the grocery store.
 
Twelve dollars for a bottle of what was essentially just another chemical sitting on our food.
 
The reviews were brutal.
 
One person asked if her bottle had gone rancid or if they'd changed the formula.
 
It smelled horrible either way.
 
And nowhere on the label did it mention parasites.
 
I even looked into buying everything organic.
 
But organic doesn't mean parasite-free.
 
Organic produce grows in the same soil.
 
Gets irrigated with the same water.
 
Gets handled by the same hands.
 
Gets shipped on the same trucks.
 
Parasites don't care if your produce is organic.
 
Every path forward had a problem.
 
Every option was incomplete.
 
I've tried EVERYTHING, I told Tom one night.
 
Nothing actually works.
 
And Lily's doctor is asking about our food.
 
Then my neighbor Sarah changed everything.
 
Sarah is a mom of two who cares about food safety the way I now cared about it.
 
Over coffee one morning, I mentioned the lump on Lily's neck, the constant anxiety about produce, the guilt every time I handed the kids a piece of fruit.
 
I asked her, how do you handle the produce thing?
 
I've tried vinegar, baking soda, those sprays, literally everything.
 
Nothing shows me it's actually working.
 
Sarah's face went serious.
 
Wait here, she said.
 
I need to show you something.
 
She reached into her bag and pulled out a small, dark navy blue capsule-shaped device.
 
It fit in the palm of her hand.
 
Barely bigger than a salt shaker.
 
Trust me, she said.
 
I tried every single thing you've tried.
 
The vinegar soak that leaves an aftertaste.
 
The baking soda mess.
 
Those sprays that are just another chemical on your food.
 
None of it kills parasites.
 
Then I found this.
 
Drop it in a bowl of water with your produce.
 
Ten minutes later you'll see everything that was hiding on your clean fruits and vegetables.
 
Pesticides. Wax. Bacteria.
 
And sometimes things you really wish you hadn't seen.
 
I was skeptical.
 
After everything I'd tried, how could something this small actually work?
 
But that afternoon, I filled a bowl with water, dropped in the strawberries I had just bought, and placed the device in the bowl.
 
I set a timer for ten minutes and went to fold laundry.
 
When I came back, I literally gasped.
 
The water had turned cloudy brown.
 
There was an oily film floating on the surface.
 
I touched it.
 
It felt waxy.
 
And floating in the water, barely visible unless you looked closely, were tiny thread-like strands.
 
I fished one out with a fork.
 
It was a worm.
 
A tiny, translucent worm that had been on the strawberries I was about to give my grandchildren.
 
Strawberries I had already rinsed under the tap.
 
I stood there staring at that bowl for a long time.
 
Not because of the wax or the cloudy water.
 
Because of the worm.
 
Because of Lily.
 
Because of all the Saturdays I'd handed her strawberries thinking I was giving her something healthy.
 
Not knowing what was clinging to the surface.
 
Not knowing what she was swallowing with every bite.
 
The small device had a label that read PurePod.
 
I immediately looked it up.
 
Turns out, it uses something called Ion Purification Technology, a scientific breakthrough originally developed for commercial food safety and industrial produce decontamination.
 
Here's how it works.
 
The device generates powerful ions that break apart pesticide residues, wax coatings, bacteria, and parasitic organisms at the molecular level.
 
The ions destroy the protective shells around parasite eggs that water, vinegar, and baking soda cannot penetrate.
 
They disrupt the cellular structure of larvae and adult parasites on contact.
 
They force everything off the surface of your produce and into the water.
 
Unlike vinegar or baking soda that only clean the outer surface, Ion Purification Technology destroys organisms that have evolved to survive everything your kitchen can throw at them.
 
It reaches what hands, brushes, and soaks never could.
 
And because nothing is added, no soaps, no sprays, no chemicals, the only byproducts are water and oxygen.
 
No aftertaste.
 
No residue.
 
No mess.
 
This same technology is widely used in commercial food processing facilities for Michelin-star restaurants, where parasite-free, chemical-free produce decontamination at scale is a critical requirement.
 
No wonder the companies selling you twelve-dollar spray bottles that go rancid and the organic industry charging a thousand dollars a year extra don't want you to know about this.
 
It makes everything they sell completely unnecessary.
 
That's why PurePod isn't in stores.
 
You won't find it at any big retailer because it cuts into their profits on replacement sprays, washes, and the organic premium.
 
It's only available on the official website.
 
The results kept getting better.
 
Berries that used to get fuzzy by Wednesday started lasting the entire week.
 
The fruit actually tasted better too.
 
Sweeter, cleaner, the way fruit is supposed to taste when it's not coated in wax and contamination.
 
Tom's stomach issues cleared up within two weeks.
 
The bloating he'd had for months disappeared.
 
He stopped reaching for the antacids after every meal.
 
The random stomach complaints that had been running through our family for months just stopped.
 
And Lily?
 
Lily's lump went down within a week.
 
The doctor said her lymph nodes were back to normal.
 
My daughter started letting her eat at grandma's house again.
 
I didn't fully realize how contaminated our produce had been until everyone stopped getting sick and the fruit started lasting twice as long.
 
I ordered two more that same week.
 
One for my daughter's house so Lily would be protected wherever she ate, and one for my travel bag because PurePod is smaller than a soda can with a battery that lasts two hundred fifty minutes.
 
It works in any bowl, any sink, any hotel room.
 
Within a month, Tom was running the Sunday produce batch himself.
 
Three neighbors had already ordered their own after I sent the dirty water photo to the group chat.
 
I didn't send the worm photo.
 
Some things you don't want to see over breakfast.
 
Since then, I've told everyone I know.
 
My sister got one.
 
My book club friends got them.
 
Every single person who's tried it has had the same reaction.
 
They can't believe they've been feeding their families produce carrying parasites, pesticide residues, and bacteria when this existed the whole time.
 
One friend told me she was spending an extra hundred and twenty dollars a month buying organic for just the Dirty Dozen items.
 
She got a PurePod and started saving money.
 
Her produce is cleaner now than organic ever was, and she's saving over a thousand dollars a year.
 
Another friend, a single grandmother raising grandchildren on a fixed income, said she'd been throwing away half her berries by Wednesday every single week.
 
PurePod solved it.
 
Her food lasts dramatically longer now, and her grandkids are eating fresher, safer meals on the same budget.
 
Right now, the company behind PurePod is offering up to seventy percent off, but I don't know how long that's going to last.
